terrain.difficultyNotes: Cannon rates on three tiers - easier, more difficult, most difficult - so percentExpert is null and the whole top third sits in percentAdvanced. The 98-trail count includes the Mittersill terrain, the lift-served but largely ungroomed area on the shoulder next door, and it includes the 21 named glades the trails-and-lifts page lists, among them Amazon, Banshee Glade, Bobcat Glade, Candyland, Echo Woods Glade and Global Warming Glade. Cannon skis appreciably harder than 33% suggests: the mountain is steep, narrow and exposed, and the difference between a groomed blue here and a groomed blue at Bretton Woods is large.

passes.name: Indy Pass
passes.access: 2 days, no blackouts, for the 2026-27 season
passes.blackouts: None. Cannon is one of the Indy resorts that takes the pass on any operating day; Indy does not publish exact 2026-27 blackout calendars until autumn 2026, but Cannon's own Indy page states no blackout dates apply.

pricing.notes: 2026-27 season. Cannon publishes no day-ticket rates at all as of the verified date - its tickets page says only that it runs peak and off-peak pricing - so all three ticket fields are null rather than estimated. The season pass figure is the Cannon-only adult (30-64) pass, which is tiered by purchase date: $799 through 4/30/26, $899 through 11/26/26, $999 through 1/31/27. The rate recorded is the one on sale on the verified date. New Hampshire residents pay markedly less - $599 / $674 / $999 on the same schedule - which is the best-value season pass in the state for anyone with an NH address. The White Mountains SuperPass, which adds Bretton Woods, Cranmore and Waterville Valley, is $1,589 through 10/31/26.

editorial.overview: Cannon is the hardest mountain in New Hampshire and it does not apologise for it. Two thousand one hundred and eighty feet of vertical, the longest drop in the state, falling down a north-facing granite face in Franconia Notch with almost nothing between the skier and the weather. It is owned by the State of New Hampshire and sits inside Franconia Notch State Park, which is why there is no village, no slopeside condominium build-out and no marketing department pretending the place is something it is not. What there is instead is an aerial tramway, a genuinely fearsome upper mountain, 21 named glades, and the Mittersill terrain next door - lift-served, largely ungroomed, and the closest thing in New Hampshire to sidecountry with a chairlift attached. The catch sits in the same sentence as the appeal. Franconia Notch funnels wind, and Cannon's exposure means ice and closures are routine rather than exceptional; on a bad day more than half the advanced terrain can be shut. The mountain rewards people who watch the forecast and drive up when it looks right, and punishes people who book a week in February and hope. If you are one of the former it is the best value in New England, especially at the New Hampshire resident pass rate, which is not far off half what an Ikon costs.
editorial.snowQuality: Cannon claims 160 inches; OnTheSnow's records say 143, and the gap is recorded as a dispute rather than averaged away. Either way this is not a big-snow mountain by Vermont standards, and it does not have the snowmaking to paper over the difference - 192 of its 287 acres are covered, leaving most of the glades and much of the steep upper terrain on natural cover only. The north-facing aspect helps what falls survive. The wind does not: Franconia Notch is a wind tunnel, the summit is scoured regularly, and icy, windswept conditions are the normal state of the upper mountain rather than a bad week. The mountain is transformed by a real storm and merely endurable without one.
editorial.crowds: Modest, and one of the strongest arguments for the place. Cannon has no slopeside lodging to fill, no destination-resort marketing budget and a reputation that filters out anyone looking for a soft day, so lift lines stay short even on Saturdays. The tramway is the exception - it is a fixed-capacity aerial lift and a tourist attraction in its own right, so it queues in a way the chairs do not. The real constraint on a Cannon day is not other skiers but the wind: when the upper mountain closes, everyone compresses onto the lower half, and a mountain that felt empty at nine can feel busy by noon. Check lift status before committing to the drive.
editorial.difficulty: Steep, narrow, exposed, and honest about it. DJ's Tramline is the signature: a narrow glade entrance that empties into a long, unrelenting fall line with sections of bare rock in it, and it is not a trail to explore on a firm day. Kinsman Glade offers the same sustained pitch in trees. The blacks off the Zoomer lift are shorter but consistently bumped, which makes them the leg-burner laps regulars actually ski. Cannon's three-tier rating puts 33% in the top tier, but the number that matters more is how much harder its blues ski than blues elsewhere - a confident intermediate from Okemo will find Cannon's middle grade a clear step up, particularly on a firm surface, which is most of the time.

keyTrails.name: DJ's Tramline
keyTrails.note: A narrow glade entrance that opens onto a long, steep, unforgiving fall line with bare rock in places. Cannon's calling card, and not a trail to sample on a firm morning.

keyTrails.name: Kinsman Glade
keyTrails.note: The same daunting sustained pitch as Tramline, in trees. One of the 21 named glades and the one that gets talked about.

keyTrails.name: Zoomer Lift Line
keyTrails.note: The blacks off the Zoomer lift are short, steep and reliably bumped. The resort's own trails page flags this one for variable conditions, which at Cannon is a meaningful warning.

keyTrails.name: Mittersill
keyTrails.note: The lift-served, largely ungroomed area on the shoulder next door, folded into Cannon's 98-trail count. The closest thing New Hampshire has to chairlift-accessed sidecountry.

keyTrails.name: Echo Woods Glade
keyTrails.note: One of the named glades running on natural cover only, which is the general condition of Cannon's tree skiing - excellent after a storm, not worth the walk without one.

tidbits: Cannon's 2,180 feet is the longest vertical drop in New Hampshire.
The mountain is owned by the State of New Hampshire and sits inside Franconia Notch State Park.
Cannon's aerial tramway is a passenger tram rather than a gondola, and runs as a summer attraction too.
New Hampshire residents buy the adult season pass for $599-$674 depending on when they commit.
Cannon is on the Indy Pass for 2026-27 with two days and no blackouts, and many published guides have not caught up.
The trails-and-lifts page names 21 separate glades, more than the mountain's acreage suggests.

dataDisputes.note: Cannon advertises 160 inches; OnTheSnow's records give 143. Seventeen inches is a material gap at a mountain whose glades depend on natural cover, and the resort's own figure is the one stored because CLAUDE.md prefers the resort's site, not because it is the better number.

moguls.policy: Cannon grooms its greens and most blues and leaves a large share of its steep terrain alone. The mountain publishes no grooming philosophy, but the practical effect of 192 snowmaking acres out of 287 is that the glades and much of the upper steep terrain live on natural snow and never see a winch cat.

namedRuns.name: Zoomer Lift Line
namedRuns.note: The blacks off the Zoomer lift are short but consistently mogully, and they are the lap regulars ski for leg burn. The resort's own trails page flags the lift line for variable conditions.

namedRuns.name: DJ's Tramline
namedRuns.note: Long, steep and ungroomed, with sections of exposed rock. It bumps up when there is enough snow on it, and frequently there is not.

namedRuns.name: Kinsman Glade
namedRuns.note: Sustained pitch in trees on natural cover. Excellent in the week after a storm, closed or unpleasant otherwise.

moguls.quality: Good when the snow is there and genuinely unpleasant when it is not, which is the honest summary of most things at Cannon. The Zoomer blacks are the dependable option - short, steep and bumped for most of the season. The bigger lines on the upper mountain are a different proposition: they need real natural cover, and Franconia Notch's wind scours the summit often enough that the troughs glaze hard. This is not a mountain to plan a bump day at in advance. It is a mountain to check the report for and drive to when it looks right.
moguls.bestTiming: A few days after a storm, once traffic has shaped the natural terrain but before the next thaw-freeze glazes it. Spring softening is the other window, and the one that makes the upper mountain reliably pleasant rather than reliably firm.
moguls.bumpCulture: No organised scene and no competitions. Cannon's culture is the Franconia Ski Club and a hard core of New Hampshire regulars who ski here because it is steep and cheap, not because there is a bump contest.

parks.overview: No terrain park is named anywhere on Cannon's site - not on the statistics page, not on the trails-and-lifts listing, and there is no park page in the sitemap. That is recorded as unpublished rather than as zero, because a mountain not writing about a park is not the same as a mountain not having one.
parks.reputation: Nobody comes to Cannon for park riding, and no third-party source consulted here mentions one either. The mountain's identity is steep natural terrain and glades; if you want built features in the White Mountains, Loon and Waterville Valley are both within forty minutes.
